progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: chem-m7-c04a (addition across a C=C: two reactants, one product; the reagent splits, one piece on each carbon; bromine water loses its colour when an alkene adds bromine; halogen prefixes with locants, for example 1,2-dibromoethane), chem-m7-c04b (alkanes react with halogens only with UV light, by substitution, with HX as a second product; UV light is energy, not a catalyst; alkynes add twice; alkenes and alkynes both decolourise bromine water, and for an open chain with one multiple bond the formula decides which), chem-m7-c03 (non-polar hydrocarbons do not mix with water and float on it; "like dissolves like"; general formulas, "no ring" condition), chem-m7-c02 ("cyclo": carbons joined in a ring; ring and alkene isomers such as cyclobutane and but-1-ene), chem-m7-p01 (risk assessment for flammable hydrocarbons; fume cupboard; organic waste). Module 6: litmus (blue turns red in acid). chem-m5-p01 and chem-m6-p02 (validity, reliability, accuracy, variables, risk assessments). Not assumed: the layer behaviour of bromine, controls in a qualitative test, accuracy for a yes-or-no test, cyclohexene by name.
progression.startsWith: Plan safe matched hydrocarbon samples and observations. The video opens: Here are two clear liquids, cyclohexane and cyclohexene. Both have a ring of six carbons, and they boil about two degrees apart. Shake each with orange bromine water.
progression.stopsAfter: planning a matched test with a water control; describing and explaining the alkene result with an addition equation and model; recognising the moved colour as a negative result; describing the substitution demonstration and its evidence with an equation; stating what a colourless result shows and its limits; judging validity, reliability and accuracy; writing the risk assessment and disposal for cyclohexane, cyclohexene and bromine water. No other addition reagents at the bench, no quantitative bromine test, no Markovnikov.

teaching.task: Shake orange bromine water with two clear liquids: in one tube the colour vanishes, in the other it only seems to. How do you run the bromine water test fairly and safely, and what does the colour change really tell you about a hydrocarbon?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) the same-looking liquids give different results, one of them misleading (1); (2) bromine adds across a C=C and is used up, so its colour goes; an alkane has no bond to open, so in the dark nothing adds; the pair differs only by one C=C (2); (3) matched volumes and the same shaking make the tubes comparable; the water control is diluted by the same amount but has nothing to react with; the white tile shows faint colour; bright light could start a slow alkane reaction and blur the comparison (3); (4) cyclohexene: the double bond opens and bromine adds, so it is used up; colourless in both layers; 1,2-dibromocyclohexane is one possible product, and other colourless addition products can form in water; with bromine in an organic solvent the dibromo compound is the one product: addition (4); (5) cyclohexane: does not mix with water, so it forms a top layer; non-polar bromine dissolves better in it than in water, so the colour moves up; the control, diluted just as much, stays clearly orange, so dilution cannot explain the pale water layer; the bromine is still there, in the top layer: no reaction (5); (6) with UV light the alkane does react, slowly, by substitution; the orange top layer from (5) is the sample, so the bromine that moved is shown to be unreacted; hydrogen bromide is an acidic gas, so damp blue litmus turns red; a strip over a tube kept in the dark changes far less, so the red is not just bromine vapour, and it is the evidence for substitution (6); (7) colourless shows a double or triple bond; alkynes react too, usually more slowly (c04b callback); not which; no change points to no double or triple bond; the formula can mislead (a ring fits CnH2n); other kinds of compounds can decolourise it too, so a quick test, not proof (7); (8) one variable changed, colour observed, the rest controlled; the matched pair and the control give validity; repeats give reliability; known samples check accuracy (8); (9) the hazards and their controls, and disposal of brominated residues (9); memory aid (10); attempts and brief feedback (11 to 14); decision rule and handoff (15); key notes (16).
teaching.conversationalApproach: orange bromine water shaken with cyclohexene loses its colour, while with cyclohexane the water also goes pale but the orange has only moved into a top layer, so the practical asks how to run the bromine water test fairly and what the colour change really tells you. Bromine adds across a C=C bond and is used up, while an alkane has nothing to add to in the dark, so the ring pair differs only by one double bond. The plan matches volumes, adds a plain water control for dilution, shakes each stoppered tube the same way against a white tile in normal room light, away from sunlight. Cyclohexene decolourises both layers within seconds by addition; cyclohexane is the trap, because non-polar bromine dissolves into the floating hydrocarbon layer, and the still-orange control rules out dilution. A teacher demonstration shows the alkane does react under UV light, with damp blue litmus turning red from hydrogen bromide as evidence of substitution. A colourless result shows a double or triple bond but not which, cyclohexane shares hexene's formula, and other compounds can decolourise it too, so it is a quick test, not proof. The variables, validity, reliability and accuracy and the risk assessment follow, and the memory aid is gone, not moved. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: Here are two clear liquids, cyclohexane and cyclohexene. Both have a ring of six carbons, and they boil about two degrees apart. Shake each with orange bromine water. In one tube, the colour vanishes. In the other, the water goes pale too, but look closer: the orange has moved into a layer on top. So how do you run this test fairly, and what does the result really tell you?
teaching.understandingCheck: (A1) "A liquid hydrocarbon, X, has the molecular formula C₅H₁₀. A student shakes an excess of X with a small volume of bromine water in a stoppered test tube, in normal room light. Two layers form: the top layer is orange and the bottom layer is pale yellow. Identify X as either pent-1-ene or cyclopentane. Justify your answer." Skeletal formulas of both shown with the names. New compounds (the scenes use C6 rings); tests the layer trap and the ring point together. Answer: cyclopentane (the colour moved into X's layer, so no C=C). Crossed mistake: "the bottom layer lost colour, so X is pent-1-ene". (A2) "In a teacher demonstration, a solution of bromine in heptane stays orange in a dark cupboard. In bright light its colour slowly fades, and the gas at the mouth of the test tube turns damp blue litmus paper red. Explain these observations. Write a balanced equation, using structural formulas, for the formation of one organic product." New alkane (the scene uses cyclohexane); tests why the dark and the light differ, the HBr evidence and the substitution equation. Answer: 2-bromoheptane + HBr (any monobromoheptane accepted; 2-bromoheptane shown because secondary hydrogens are substituted preferentially). Crossed mistake: "C₇H₁₆Br₂" (an addition product; there is no bond to open). Neither attempt repeats chem-m7-g01's Q4 (evaluating "it decolourised, so it is an alkene"), which follows next.
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017), as printed: "investigate, write equations and construct models to represent the reactions of unsaturated hydrocarbons when added to a range of chemicals, including but not limited to:; hydrogen (H2); halogens (X2); hydrogen halides (HX); water (H2O) (ACSCH136)" "investigate, write equations and construct models to represent the reactions of saturated hydrocarbons when substituted with halogens" "describe the procedures required to safely handle and dispose of organic substances (ACSCH075)" This practical covers the halogen (X₂) investigation for the first dotpoint (the other reagents were chem-m7-c04a and c04b, where their conditions put them outside a student bench: pressurised hydrogen with a nickel catalyst, steam at about 300 °C), and the investigation half of the second. this video prepares students to plan, carry out and interpret the bromine water test; it does not claim that watching it is conducting it. It teaches: why cyclohexane and cyclohexene are a fair pair (same ring, same carbon count, one C=C the only difference); matched volumes, a water control for dilution, the same shaking, a white tile, normal room light and reading at once; the alkene result (colour gone from both layers within seconds) and its equation with structural formulas, built as a model; the alkane result and its trap (bromine dissolves better in the hydrocarbon, so the colour moves into the top layer: moved, not gone), read against the control; the alkane's slow substitution with bromine under UV light as a teacher demonstration, using the orange cyclohexane layer from the test (no liquid bromine), with damp blue litmus turning red, compared with a strip over a tube kept in the dark, as the evidence for hydrogen bromide, and its equation; what a colourless result can and cannot show (a C=C or C≡C; alkynes too, usually more slowly; not which; a ring with the alkene formula does not react; other kinds of compounds can decolourise bromine water too, so it is a quick test, not proof); the variables, validity, reliability and accuracy for a yes-or-no test; the risk assessment and disposal. Not re-taught: why a C=C adds and an alkane does not, addition against substitution, UV light as an energy source rather than a catalyst, alkyne two-step addition, general formulas (chem-m7-c03, c04a, c04b; recalled in one clause each, "as in the last video"); "like dissolves like" (chem-m7-c03, one clause). Not here: hydrogenation, hydrohalogenation and hydration as bench work (chem-m7-c04a; conditions unsuitable for a student bench); ethyne generation (calcium carbide; not a student practical; alkynes stay a spoken limit); Markovnikov's rule; naming the bromo-alcohol product of bromine water (scene 4 says only "other colourless addition products"; author note c); the quantitative bromine test (measured amounts; site correction recorded by c04b); IR or NMR; Module 8 analysis (Module 8 P05 refers back here).
